staged_description.description_long: In 1953, Senator Joseph McCarthy hired Roy Cohn as chief counsel to the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations. PBS’s American Experience account says McCarthy relied heavily on Cohn for contacts, information, ideas, and political advice. Cohn had recently gained public prominence as a prosecutor in the espionage case against Julius and Ethel Rosenberg. In his new role, he helped McCarthy conduct investigations into alleged communist influence in government and public life during the Red Scare. The committee’s investigations and McCarthy’s tactics became closely associated with the term McCarthyism. Historical accounts describe Cohn as an influential aide, while the available sources do not establish that he invented McCarthyism or acted as its sole architect. This appointment took place decades before Donald Trump’s political career and has no documented connection to him. The event is Cohn’s appointment and influence within McCarthy’s committee, situated in the broader history of the Red Scare.
